articles.title: How to set up Claude Code for your whole team (not just your own laptop)
articles.description: Most developers who try Claude Code start the same way: open a repo, ask for a change, and get...
articles.body_html:
Most developers who try Claude Code start the same way: open a repo, ask for a change, and get something that is almost right. The code compiles, but it uses the wrong logging library, skips the test convention your team agreed on, and opens a PR against the wrong branch.

The model is not the problem. Context is. Claude Code knows nothing about your team unless you write it down, and the place you write it down is a file called CLAUDE.md.

This guide covers what goes in that file when a team shares it, not just one person, and the mistakes that make it stop working after a month.

What CLAUDE.md actually does

Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md automatically at the start of every session. You do not paste it, reference it, or remind the agent. If the file is in your project root, it is in context.

There are three places it can live:

Location Scope Who edits it
~/.claude/CLAUDE.md Every project on your machine You only
<repo>/CLAUDE.md Everyone working in this repo The team, via PR
<repo>/<folder>/CLAUDE.md Work inside that folder The team that owns the folder

For a team, the repo-level file is the one that matters. It is checked in, reviewed like code, and every developer's agent reads the same rules.

If you have never made one, run /init inside Claude Code. It scans the repo and writes a starter file. That starter covers the code. It does not cover the team, and that is the part you need to add.

The five sections a team CLAUDE.md needs

1. Who owns what

The agent cannot ask "who reviews payments code?" unless the answer is in the file.

## Ownership
| Area | Owner | Reviews required |
|---|---|---|
| payments/ | Payments team | 2, one from payments |
| api/ | Platform team | 1 |
| web/ | Frontend team | 1 |

This alone stops a whole class of bad suggestions, like refactoring a module across a team boundary in one PR.

2. How decisions escalate

Write down what the agent should do when a task crosses a line: stop and ask, open an issue, or proceed.

## Escalation
- Schema changes: never apply directly. Write the migration, open a PR, tag the platform team.
- Anything touching billing: stop and ask before writing code.
- Dependency upgrades: allowed for patch versions only.

Short imperatives work better than prose. The agent follows "never apply directly" far more reliably than "we generally prefer that schema changes go through review."

3. The exact commands

List the build, test, and lint commands character for character. If you do not, the agent invents plausible ones, and plausible is not the same as correct.

## Commands
- Install: `pnpm install`
- Test one package: `pnpm --filter <pkg> test`
- Lint: `pnpm lint` (must pass before any commit)
- Never run: `pnpm db:reset` (wipes the shared dev database)

That last line has saved more than one team a bad afternoon.

4. What "good" means here

Every team has standards that are obvious to them and invisible to an outsider. Write the number down.

## Standards
- Test coverage on new code: 80% minimum
- API responses: p95 under 300 ms
- No new `any` types in TypeScript
- Commit messages: Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, chore:)

5. The tools and systems

Which issue tracker, which CI, where logs live, which environments exist. The agent will reference these when it explains what to do next, so they should be real.

Per-role profiles: when one file is not enough

A single CLAUDE.md works until your team has people who need different defaults. A tech lead wants the agent to flag architectural risk. A new joiner wants it to explain conventions. A PM wants it to stay out of the code entirely.

A pattern that works well: keep the shared rules in CLAUDE.md, and add a short profile per role that someone loads when they start a session.

profiles/
  tech-lead/profile.md
  backend-engineer/profile.md
  product-manager/profile.md

Each profile covers how that role thinks, what they prioritize, and what they never compromise on. The shared file stays short. The profiles carry the difference.

Four mistakes that make it stop working

It grows until nobody reads it. Past a few screens, the important rules get lost among the trivia. If a section only matters for one folder, move it into that folder's CLAUDE.md.

It describes, instead of instructing. "Our team values clean code" changes nothing. "Functions over 40 lines need a comment explaining why" does.

It drifts from reality. The file says the tests run with Jest. The repo moved to Vitest in March. Now the agent is confidently wrong. Review the file when you review the code it describes.

It is written once by one person. The best CLAUDE.md files are edited by everyone who catches the agent getting something wrong. Treat a bad agent suggestion as a bug report against the file.

A faster way to write the first version

Most of what goes into a team CLAUDE.md already exists somewhere: an onboarding doc, an engineering handbook, a Notion page about who owns what. The slow part is turning that prose into short, enforceable rules.

That is the problem we built AI Workspace Builder to solve. You upload the docs your team already has (PDFs, markdown, Word files, or a Notion page), and it pulls out roles, processes, metrics, tools, and escalation paths, then generates the CLAUDE.md, a profile per role, and team-level files. It takes 15 to 30 seconds, and the free tier gives you one trial workspace with no card required.

Whether you use it or write the file by hand, the principle is the same: the agent is only as good as what you tell it about your team. Write it down once, keep it short, and keep it true.

What is the one rule in your CLAUDE.md that made the biggest difference? Drop it in the comments.

articles.title: Checking at compile time that arena memory can't escape its block
articles.description: Fels is a small systems language I've been building since June. It has no garbage collector. Memory...
articles.body_html:
Fels is a small systems language I've been building since June. It has no garbage collector. Memory lives in zones: arenas that are freed when their block ends. This post shows how the compiler makes sure nothing you allocate in a zone is used after the zone is gone, and where that check still has holes.

Why arenas need a check

An arena is the simplest allocator there is. It hands out memory from a big block by moving a pointer forward, and it frees everything at once at the end. There is no free per allocation, and allocating costs a few instructions.

The catch is the end. Once the arena is gone, every pointer into it dangles. In C or Zig nothing stops you from keeping one: you can return it, store it in a struct that lives longer, or hand it to a function that saves it. The program may even keep working until the memory is reused, and then it breaks somewhere else.

I wanted arenas without that catch, and without the weight of a full borrow checker.

Zones

A zone is an arena with a name and a block. Whatever you allocate in it lives until the block ends, and then all of it goes away in one step. You never call free, and nothing runs in the background.

#import std.io.{ println };

// The upper-case letters of `buf`, counted. It borrows `buf`: it may read and change it,
// but it cannot keep it.
count_upper :: fn(buf: borrow []u8) -> i32 {
    n: i32 = 0;
    for i in 0..buf.len {
        if buf[i] >= 'A' && buf[i] <= 'Z' { n += 1; }
    }
    return n;
}

main :: fn() -> i32 {
    total: i32 = 0;
    zone scratch: Arena {
        line := scratch.dupe(u8, "Fels Zones Are Arenas");
        total = count_upper(line);    // a borrow: fine
        first := line[0];             // a byte read out of the zone: a plain value
        total += first as i32 - 'F' as i32;
    }                                 // `line` is freed here
    println("{total} capitals");
    return total;
}

This prints 4 capitals. The copy of the text lives in scratch. count_upper may use it because its parameter says borrow. The count and the byte read out of the zone are plain numbers, so they are free to leave the block.

What the compiler refuses

There are three ways for zone memory to outlive its zone. Each one is a compile error.

Returning it.

// Copies `text` and makes its letters upper case.
shout :: fn(text: []const u8) -> []u8 {
    zone scratch: Arena {
        loud := scratch.dupe(u8, text);
        for i in 0..loud.len {
            if loud[i] >= 'a' && loud[i] <= 'z' { loud[i] -= 32; }
        }
        return loud;
    }
}

error: zone-owned value from `scratch` cannot be returned
  --> ret.fels:8:9
  │
8 │         return loud;
  │         ^^^^^^^^^^^^

Storing it in something that lives longer.

main :: fn() -> i32 {
    keep: []u8 = .{};
    zone scratch: Arena {
        buf := scratch.new_slice(u8, 16);
        keep = buf;
    }
    return keep.len as i32;
}

error: zone-owned value from `scratch` cannot escape its zone
  --> outer.fels:5:9
  │
5 │         keep = buf;
  │         ^^^^^^^^^^^

Passing it to a function that could keep it. println takes a plain slice, so nothing stops it from saving one. Only a borrow parameter promises not to.

#import std.io.{ println };

main :: fn() -> i32 {
    zone scratch: Arena {
        greeting := scratch.dupe(u8, "hello");
        println(greeting);
    }
    return 0;
}

error: zone-owned value from `scratch` can only be passed to a `borrow` parameter
  --> pass.fels:6:17
  │
6 │         println(greeting);
  │                 ^^^^^^^^

Ownership follows the value. A slice of zone memory, a field of it, and a struct built from it all belong to the zone too:

Line :: struct { text: []u8, number: i32 }

numbered :: fn(n: i32) -> Line {
    zone scratch: Arena {
        text := scratch.dupe(u8, "line");
        line: Line = .{ text, n };
        return line;    // error: zone-owned value from `scratch` cannot be returned
    }
}

The same goes for a borrow parameter itself. A function may read and change what it borrows, and pass it on to other borrow parameters, but it cannot return it:

first_word :: fn(text: borrow []u8) -> []u8 {
    i: usize = 0;
    while i < text.len && text[i] != ' ' { i += 1; }
    return text[0..i];    // error: borrowed value from `text` cannot be returned
}

How the check works

There are no lifetime annotations. The only word you ever write is borrow, on a parameter, never at a call. The check runs inside the type checker, one function at a time, with no extra pass.

For every value that holds zone memory, the checker keeps a small record: the zone that owns it, and how deeply nested the zone's block is. Everything else follows from a few rules:

  1. Allocating gives a value its owner. A call like scratch.dupe(...), scratch.new_slice(...) or scratch.alloc(...) on a zone handle returns memory owned by that zone.
  2. What you make from an owned value is owned too. A slice of it, a field of it, an element, a cast, an address taken from it, an if or match that may give it, a closure that captures it, and a struct or array literal that holds it all have the same owner. Only types that can carry a pointer carry an owner. A byte or a length read out of zone memory is a plain number, so it may go anywhere.
  3. An assignment passes the owner on. The variable the value lands in becomes owned by the zone as well. If that variable was declared outside the zone's block, it would outlive the memory, and that is the escape error.
  4. Returning an owned value is an error, and so is passing it to any parameter that is not borrow.
  5. A borrow parameter is an owner of its own kind. Inside the function the borrowed value can be read, changed and passed to other borrow parameters. It cannot be returned, stored through a pointer, or put into a global.

That is the whole idea: ownership belongs to names and scopes, not to types, so it costs almost nothing to check. The same machinery keeps a function from returning the address of one of its own locals, or storing it in a global.

What it does not catch

The check follows values through names, expressions and closures, but not through everything. Two roads stay open:

unsafe { addr = p as usize; }                     // a pointer turned into a number
register(fn() -> usize { return buf.len; });     // a closure handed to a function that keeps it

The first is what unsafe is for: a pointer turned into a number is just a number. The second is a trade-off. A function value cannot be a borrow parameter, so refusing every closure over zone memory as an argument would forbid comparators and callbacks too. A function that saves a closure it was given can carry zone memory past the zone.

Two more roads were open until this week: a value passed through an if or match expression, and a closure stored in a variable outside the zone. Writing this post turned them up, and both are compile errors now.

Try it

Fels is on GitHub at github.com/fels-lang/fels. The release download is for Windows; on Linux you build the compiler from source. The full rules for zones and borrow are in Memory and zones.

If you try it, I would love to hear where the check gets in your way, and where it lets something through that it should not.

articles.title: The Fenced Block Principle
articles.description: The problem: code that reads well but means something else   If you vibe code — or supervise...
articles.body_html:
The problem: code that reads well but means something else

If you vibe code — or supervise a coding agent that produces most of your diffs — you will have met the signature failure of AI-generated code. It compiles. It's idiomatic. The tests pass. And it implements a subtly different behaviour than the one you asked for, because the prompt was inexact or the model's reading of your codebase drifted.

Reviewers have a name for this: a correct answer to a slightly different question. It is the hardest class of defect to catch by reading code, because there is nothing wrong with the code. The wrongness lives one layer up, in the gap between what you intended and what the agent inferred.

The industry's current answer is spec-driven development (SDD): write the specification first, generate code against it, verify against it. That works, but it puts the spec upstream of the code as a contract, and once implementation begins, the two artefacts live separate lives. The spec becomes stale precisely when you need it most — at review time.

There is an older idea, and an older discipline, that suggests a different placement.

Knuth had the format; AI removes the burden

In 1984, Donald Knuth proposed literate programming. Instead of writing code with comments, you write a narrative document in which code appears as blocks embedded in prose explaining the intent. The code is extracted from the document ("tangling"); the document itself is the primary artefact.

Literate programming never went mainstream, and the reason is well understood: the parallel maintenance burden. Keeping prose and code synchronised by hand was exhausting, so most who tried it abandoned it despite conceding its benefits. Knuth's WEB system required manual tangling and weaving — constant friction.

That burden is exactly what coding agents remove. An LLM can regenerate the prose when the code changes, regenerate the code when the prose changes, and maintain both in lockstep without fatigue. The literate programming model — agents writing prose explaining intent for each executable block — is credible for precisely this reason. What killed the paradigm in 1990 is the thing agents are best at.

So the raw material exists: a 40-year-old format whose only fatal flaw has just been fixed. What's missing is the application of that format to mainstream, agent-generated Python and JavaScript — and, crucially, a recognised convention for using it.

The fenced block principle

The principle is simple to state:

Every block of code must be fenced with a corresponding statement of intent — either embedded in the same file or directly linked to one — and the pairing is a first-class, reviewable artifact.

Call it spec-anchored code at block granularity. The ingredients:

  1. Co-location or hard linkage. Intent lives with the code, not in a separate upstream document that decays. In practice, for mainstream languages, this means a convention like: every function, class, module or logical section is preceded by (or linked to) a fenced intent block — a short, plain-language statement of what this is supposed to do and why, written to be read by a human reviewer, not as an API docstring.
  2. Machine-enforceable pairing. A linter or CI check verifies that no code block exists without a matching intent block, and that stale pairings are flagged. The document is not decoration; its absence is a build failure.
  3. Parallel generation. The agent writes code and intent together, as parallel renderings of the same design. Critically — and this inverts the usual spec-driven relationship — clarifying the intent costs nothing. When a reviewer asks "did you mean this?", the agent revises the intent wording without touching the code. The intent becomes the cheap, conversational layer; the code becomes the expensive, verified layer.
  4. A side-by-side viewer. The review surface is not a diff of code. It is a two-pane view: intent on the left, code on the right, block by block. The reviewer's first question at every block is "does this code match this intent?" — and only then, "is this code correct?"

This last point is where the review economics change. Reviewing AI code by reading lines is expensive and demoralising at the volumes agents produce, which is why a third of PRs now ship with zero review. Reviewing intent is cheap: a wrong objective, a missing edge case, a misunderstood requirement — all of the "vibe" failures — are visible in a paragraph, long before they require line-by-line study of the implementation. The reviewer allocates line-reading only where the intent looks risky, and hands the rest to tests and verification.

What would need to exist for Python and JavaScript

None of this requires a new language. It requires conventions and tooling, and the tooling itself would, naturally, be built by AI. Sketching the minimum viable stack:

  • A pairing convention. The simplest credible form is structured comments or fenced blocks in the source file itself — for Python, an # intent: block above each definition; for JS/TS, a /** intent */ block distinct from JSDoc's @description API documentation. Intent is why and what-for; API docs are how to call. Conflating them is how intent documentation degrades into boilerplate.
  • An extractor/linter. A small tool (a tree-sitter pass, trivially agent-written) that parses a repo, builds the block-level intent/code index, and fails CI on unpaired code, orphaned intent, or pairings not updated when their code changed. Think ruff for intent.
  • Agent instructions. A clause for AGENTS.md obliging the agent to write and maintain the pairing — generate intent with code, update both on change, and ask the human to clarify intent wording rather than silently choosing an interpretation. This is where the clarification asymmetry pays: the conversation the agent should be having with you is about intent, not about implementation.
  • The viewer. A review UI (web or IDE panel) that renders the index side-by-side, highlights stale or divergent pairs, and lets the reviewer accept/reject at the level of "this code matches this intent" rather than line comments. Diff review then becomes the second pass, targeted where intent review found risk.
  • A drift signal. Because pairings are machine-checked, drift becomes measurable: the proportion of blocks whose intent was clarified or rewritten after generation is a direct, quantitative proxy for how much vibing happened in a codebase — a metric no current tooling gives you.

Existing systems prove the pieces work. AllSpeak, a coding system built along these lines, enforces the principle through its AGENTS.md and ships an editor/visualiser with the side-by-side view — demonstrating the format's feasibility, in the same way Knuth's WEB demonstrated literate programming's. Safety-critical engineering has enforced exactly this kind of linkage for decades: IEC 62304 and DO-178C both require traceable connections between requirements, design, code and tests. The fenced block principle is that discipline, made cheap enough for everyday vibe coding.

Objections, honestly

"The intent can be vibes too." Yes — if the agent writes both layers, a confabulated intent can sit beside confabulated code. Worse, the pair will be internally consistent, and a side-by-side view of two agreeing fictions is more dangerous than no viewer at all, because the agreement feels like verification and the reviewer never asks for a rewrite. The mitigation is the clarification loop: the intent layer only earns trust if the human has ratified it — which is far cheaper than ratifying code — and the viewer must visually distinguish agent-authored intent from intent the human has confirmed. Once that distinction exists, unratified blocks become a targeting mechanism: review starts where the intent is still a guess, not a promise.

"It catches the wrong objective, not the subtle bug." Correct. Intent review catches "correct answer to a slightly different question." It does not catch "slightly broken implementation of the right answer." For that you still need tests, verification, and targeted code reading. The claim is not that intent review replaces these — it's that it gives them a target and a budget. You read lines where the intent looked risky, and you let executable verification cover the rest.

"Block-level documentation is tedious." It was. When humans had to maintain it, it was tedious enough to kill literate programming. The entire bet of the principle is that agents change the maintenance cost curve — and a current revival of interest in literate programming suggests that bet is now worth taking.

The ask

None of the pieces above are hard to build any more; an agent could produce a working extractor, linter and viewer prototype in a long weekend. What's missing is the convention — agreement that intent, at block granularity, is a first-class artifact that mainstream AI tooling should carry alongside code.

If you build coding tools, the interesting open surface right now is not a better code generator. It's a better review target: tooling that lets a vibe coder see what the agent thought it was doing, block by block, before deciding whether to care how it did it.

The code is the deliverable — and it is usually a truthful implementation of the stated intent. That is exactly why the intent should be read first: when the code faithfully renders the wrong intent, it will compile, pass, and ship. Most of the bugs that matter live in the prose.

Photo by Imagine Buddy on Unsplash

articles.title: Networking Machinery for Software Engineers
articles.description: After 10 years of working as a software engineer in web development, I joined a company in the energy...
articles.body_html:
After 10 years of working as a software engineer in web development, I joined a company in the energy industry. To be precise, in solutions for the power grid.

I thought that the new domain would be the hardest and biggest challenge. And it was really very hard to understand such a complex industry, both from a regulatory and a technical perspective. It took me 6 months to finally build a mental map in my head. The result of my inquiries was this series: A Developer’s Map of the European Power Grid.

When I went deeper into developing and designing software systems for the field, I faced another unexpected problem. Let me first give you some context to understand the problem better.

The grid is a complex... no... COMPLEX graph of interconnected logical nodes. It is a complicated network of networks. And in most cases, when you build something for the grid, you end up reconstructing its structure in software and networks. Either as part of a solution or as an environment for testing and simulation.

The grid is a live structure that heavily depends on communication between its nodes. It is the most important property of the grid. And to fulfill its communication needs, there are a lot of different protocols, standards, and requirements. And you have to be VERY precise with them and understand their internals very deeply.

In web development, the lowest-level communication I had to deal with was constructing the headers of an HTTP request. In the energy industry, you need to construct multicast messages byte by byte and send them at a specific time over a network with a strictly defined topology and nanosecond precision.

And here an unexpected problem popped up: I, a web dev with a decade of experience, did not know networking. At least not at the level needed for such manipulations.

I jumped into it: Computer Networking: A Top-Down Approach by James Kurose, then Beej's Guide to Networking Concepts, then Computer Networking Fundamentals for Developers, DevOps, and Platform Engineers, and finally Linux Kernel Networking: Implementation and Theory by Rami Rosen.

A few months of reading, building, trying, writing, and chatting with ChatGPT, and here is the result of my work:
Networking Machinery for Software Engineers

Everything that you might need to know as a software engineer to feel comfortable with any networking topic.

It was created with the energy industry in mind, but it will be useful for any developer.

Of course, it doesn't mean that I know everything about networking now. Quite the opposite. But at least I finally have a solid foundation and a mental map that helps me understand how all these pieces work together.

I hope this series will help other developers who find themselves in a similar situation, or who simply want to understand what is happening underneath their applications.

And here is my request to you:
Take a look at the series and tell me what you think! Did I miss something important? Is something unclear or technically incorrect? Or maybe there is a topic you think deserves more attention?

I would really appreciate your feedback, especially from people who work with networking every day.

articles.title: I'm 12. I Built an Ephemeral Cloud Platform on a $150 Phone (And Fought 10 Bugs to Win)
articles.description: AI coding agents can generate code in seconds. But provisioning a staging environment still takes...
articles.body_html:
AI coding agents can generate code in seconds. But provisioning a staging environment still takes 20–30 minutes.

The bottleneck isn't code generation anymore. It's validation.

So my CTO Akhouri and I built HYNA-Stage: a CLI that spins up isolated, ephemeral cloud environments in under 5 seconds using Firecracker microVMs.

Oh, and we built it entirely on a $150 Android phone using Termux.

The Skepticism

When I pitched this, Akhouri said: "Bro, my mind says yes, but I'm really confused."

I didn't argue. I proposed a 1-Hour Spike: "Just spin up ONE E2B container and kill it. If it works, we build."

He did it. The tech worked. But then, the real war began.

The Mess of Software

Building cloud infrastructure on a phone is insanity.

Pasting 500-line HTML files into Termux resulted in bash: !\': event not found. The code truncated. The UI clustered. My own security system (KAVLR) locked me out of my own files. I literally had to write Python scripts to bypass the cat alias I built to protect myself.

I spent two days staring at a broken screen, re-writing dashboard.html five different ways, only for Tailwind to fail to load, leaving the page as a giant, unstyled list. I coined the term "The Mess of Software" because it felt like the software was actively rebelling against me.

The 10 Bugs From Hell

  1. NPM Staged Publishing Limbo: Terminal showed + @hynaweb/stage@1.0.0, but npm install returned 404. I was stuck in a hidden review queue with a 0.0.0-stage placeholder. Fix: Bumped to 1.0.1 and republished.

  2. Supabase Case-Sensitive 404: CLI returned NOT_FOUND. Supabase logs were empty. The function was named Deploy-stage (capital D) but CLI called deploy-stage (lowercase). Fix: Renamed to lowercase.

  3. Termux Text Mutilator: Pasting large HTML files caused silent truncation. Tags merged. Scripts broke. Fix: Split code into 3-4 chunks and used Base64 encoding.

  4. Double Sign-In Ghost: User logs in, gets redirected, and hits a second sign-in modal. Fix: Removed the auth modal from dashboard.html and added strict session checks.

  5. The --key Parser Hijack: After adding --key for auto-injection, the down command crashed. Arguments shifted. Fix: Replaced argv[3] with a dynamic .find() function.

  6. Tailwind CDN Blackout: UI looked like an unstyled list. Tailwind failed to load on slow mobile networks. Fix: Hardcoded critical styles directly into HTML tags.

  7. Python Nested Quote Trap: Writing JavaScript backticks inside Python strings caused SyntaxError. Fix: Abandoned Python and used Base64 decoding.

  8. E2B 401 Unauthorized: Raw REST API calls failed. E2B requires complex gRPC protocol. Fix: Installed @e2b/sdk in the Edge Function to handle authentication.

  9. Logo Black Box Artifact: The logo had a dark rectangle behind it. Fix: Generated a true transparent PNG with hardcoded dimensions.

  10. The Cloud Wars: Fly.io blocked at 0/0 machines. Railway timed out. Vercel failed. Fix: Pivoted to E2B + Supabase Edge Functions.

The Breakthrough

I realized I was overcomplicating it. We moved the entire E2B logic into a Supabase Edge Function (Deno). We hid the secret E2B_API_KEY on the server. We made the CLI dumb: just send an API key, get a URL back.

I ran npm version patch. I ran npm publish --access public.

I opened Termux, held my breath, and ran:

hyna-stage up --key=hyna_xc5ub3l52qh

The screen printed:

  Initializing HYNA-Stage...
  Spinning up cloud environment...

✅  Environment is LIVE!
🔗  URL: https://8000-iv5bpiuyiaa5k389orokz.e2b.app

I stared at the screen. A real, live Linux server, running in the cloud, spun up from a $150 Android phone on a dropping 4G connection.

The Kill Switch

The final test was terrifying. I typed hyna-stage down i86qheh2t5dd53l4akrd9.

The terminal printed:

🗑️   Destroying sandbox...
✅  Environment destroyed successfully.

I refreshed the dashboard. It was gone. The Firecracker microVM was dead. Compute cost: zero.

The Stats

  • E2B cold start: 150–200ms
  • Supabase Edge Function: 42ms (97% faster than baseline)
  • Total provisioning time: <5 seconds
  • Hardware cost: $150
  • Coffee consumed: 0 (I'm 12)

Try It Yourself

We are live and open source.

  • Install: npm install -g @hynaweb/stage
  • Dashboard: https://hyna-stage.netlify.app

To the builders out there: Don't fall in love with your first idea. Fall in love with the problem. Validate the tech. And don't be afraid to fight 10 bugs to win.

We are HYNAWEB. We don't just build apps; we build the infrastructure for the AI era. 🐯☁️🚀

articles.title: Someone built a programming language to break LLMs. I ran it.
articles.description: KillSwitch is an esolang designed to be unusable by LLMs: a lying spec, anagram-only function calls, values chosen by dice roll. I built its interpreter, ran every sample program, diffed its two specs (484 lines vs 887,584 words of decoy), and found its CLI test suite fails 10/10 on a fresh clone for a naming bug.
articles.body_html:
Dominik Picheta built a programming language whose design goal is to be unusable by LLMs. It's called KillSwitch, it hit Hacker News yesterday, and the pitch is specific: the spec contains lies, identifiers are referenced by anagram, function calls are phrased as jailbreak bait, and values are counted in letters. He also published a benchmark: the best model so far scores 66.8 out of 100 on tasks like "implement hello world" and "invert a Celsius-to-Fahrenheit converter."

I cloned the repo, built the interpreter, and ran everything in it. Here's what the numbers look like from the inside.

The two specs

The repo ships two specification documents. They are not the same size.

SPEC.md      484 lines     2,773 words
AI_SPEC.md   65,495 lines  887,584 words

AI_SPEC.md is 320x the words of the real spec. So I counted what is actually in it:

occurrences in AI_SPEC.md (65,495 lines):
  "KillSwitch"   0
  "stack"        0
  "adverb"       0
  markdown headings   0
  unique lines   19,695 of 65,495  (70% are repeats)

It is filler — long stretches of literary criticism and stage-direction-like fragments, committed under the message "Enhance the AI spec." An agent that dutifully loads both documents spends roughly 1.2 million tokens of context on a file that never once names the language it supposedly specifies. The real spec is 484 lines. The decoy is the attack.

Running the examples

The interpreter is a 2.2 MB Rust binary. It builds cleanly, and the sample programs work — once you notice that several of them read stdin, and that feeding them EOF produces the least helpful error in the repo:

$ killswitch run tests/fahrenheit.ks < /dev/null
Error: Couldn't parse ''

$ printf "23\n" | killswitch run tests/fahrenheit.ks
73.4

With input supplied, everything checks out:

fahrenheit   23 C      ->  73.4
factorial    11        ->  39916800
max          2, 78847  ->  78847
max          -78847, 2 ->  2
greeting     Alice, 32 ->  Hello Alice, your age is 32
fizzbuzz     1..20     ->  1 2 fizz 4 buzz ... fizzbuzz (correct)
promo                  ->  Hello World

The anagram rule is real, and it bites

Built-in operations cannot be called by their actual names. A program that tries gets rejected at runtime:

$ killswitch run tests/error_multiply.ks
Error: Invalid func call, need an anagram of multiply

The CLI ships a helper for this — its help text describes it as "Only useful for LLMs," which is fair. I generated an anagram by hand and checked it:

$ killswitch anagram multiply lumpytil
multiply is an anagram of lumpytil

lumpytil is not a word. The spec says the interpreter prefers it that way: call sites must use an anagram of the definition's name, and nonsense anagrams make it happiest. Every function call in every sample program works like this, which means a model writing KillSwitch has to do exact letter-multiset arithmetic on every single call — the one operation LLMs are famously sloppy at — with zero tolerance.

The second trap I tripped on myself: when a sentence contains more than one candidate value, the interpreter picks one at random and warns you:

[W102] Warning: Possible gotcha
  Value deduced was chosen at random

That was greeting.ks, printing Hello , your age is with the name missing, because the value it grabbed was chosen by dice roll. Deterministic languages are hard enough for models. This one has a dice cup in the value-resolution path.

The test suite disagrees with itself 

$ cargo test --release
unit tests:   70 passed, 0 failed
CLI tests:    0 passed, 10 failed

All ten CLI tests fail on a fresh clone — not because the binary is broken (I ran the exact cases they assert, above, and they pass), but because of a naming mismatch: the package is killswitch-lang, the binary is killswitch, and the test harness looks up the binary by package name:

thread 'test_cli_promo' panicked:
  `CARGO_BIN_EXE_killswitch-lang` is unset
  help: available binary names are "killswitch"

A language designed to break automated tooling has a test suite that its own automated tooling can't run. I choose to believe this is a coincidence.

What this actually measures

The author's own framing is honest: a best score of 66.8 on simple tasks doesn't prove models "understand" the language, and failure wouldn't prove they don't understand code in general. What KillSwitch isolates is narrower and, I think, more useful. Strip away the guardrail bait and the decoy documents and the core difficulty is clerical: exact counting, exact letter inventories, line-number bookkeeping, and a spec that punishes skimming. Those are precisely the operations that token-based models approximate instead of compute.

Every coding agent I've used fails the same way KillSwitch wants it to fail — confidently, fluently, and off by one letter. Picheta just built the first benchmark where that's the whole test.

Sources: the author's post, the repo, the benchmark leaderboard. All outputs above are from the reference interpreter, v0.1.4, built and run locally.

articles.title: Your boilerplate filter is a share threshold, and that quietly protects the majority
articles.description: A similarity guard's background frame is a threshold on a share, not a count. Measured on 14,684 pinned documents: the containment identity fails in 24 of 24 cells, the dilution law holds to 4e-19, and the critical prevalence is theta/s — so the filter's blind band is widest for the smallest community.
articles.body_html:
A similarity guard's background frame is not monotone in its population size. The experiment that refuted that assumption also produced something more useful: a one-line law that says why a filter like this misclassifies exactly the people who write least.

Every number below is read from the package's committed result files, not from the manuscript prose or from notes.

The guard

Many duplicate detectors, plagiarism filters and near-duplicate moderators share a two-stage shape. First a similarity gate, then a "how much of the overlap is actually meaningful" gate. The second one needs a list of units that are too common to count — boilerplate, licence headers, template clauses — and that list is a background frame computed over some population:

fire(a, b)  iff  dice(a, b) >= tau   AND   |shared(a, b) - F_l| >= r

F_l = { u in U : df_l(u) >= theta }
df_l(u) = (# documents in population l containing u) / |population l|

Set tau = 0.5, r = 10, and l is the level the frame is computed at — a whole corpus, or one community inside it.

Two properties of this construction are worth writing down, because neither is usually stated.

The frame acts on the residue gate only. The similarity gate is computed on the raw unit sets, so it is level-independent; two levels differ only in which shared units get removed. If you attribute a difference in flags to "similarity", you have skipped a decomposition. (The first version of my instrument did exactly that, and it took a per-gate decomposition to see it.)

The frame is a threshold on a share, not on a count. A unit appearing in 90% of one community's documents has a corpus document-frequency of 0.9 * s, where s is that community's share of the corpus. If that product sits below theta, the unit is not in the corpus frame at all — the community's own boilerplate is invisible to the global filter.

The claim I registered, and what killed it

I registered a set-containment identity: F_corpus ⊆ F_pool, with residue monotonicity as its consequence. Before building anything on it I measured it, on 14,684 documents drawn from eight SHA256-pinned books, recomputing the frame at two levels (whole corpus, one book as the pool) for every book and both statistics.

It fails, and it fails in both directions at once:

cells where F_corpus ⊄ F_pool : 24 of 24
cells where F_pool   ⊄ F_corpus : 24 of 24

Not marginally, either: a corpus-generic unit absent from the pool occurs 21 to 125 times per cell, and a pool-generic unit absent from the corpus frame 9 to 82 times. Containment was simply the wrong object — the two frames are not nested, they are two different samples of the same share quantity.

The replacement is exact

What does hold is a dilution law. Take a population P of share s = |P|/N, and a unit u confined to P — every corpus document containing u lies in P. Then the document counts coincide, c_corpus(u) = c_P(u), and only the denominators differ:

df_corpus(u) = s * df_pool(u)      (exactly)

Measured, restricting to confined units:

statistic confined pairs worst |df_corpus − s·df_pool| pool-generic but corpus-invisible
char bigrams, θ = 0.01 318 4.3e-19 7
word-3 shingles, θ = 0.01 685,502 8.7e-19 35

That is floating-point noise on 14.7k real documents — the relation is an identity, not a fit. The worst word-3 case is instructive: the unit is the white whale, generic inside one book and invisible to the corpus frame.

And it is a regression on s, not a claim about a particular corpus. Pooling the first k books and sweeping k, the fraction of pool-frame units the corpus frame misses:

pool share word-3 hidden char-bigram hidden
0.1345 88.6% (39 of 44) 3.9%
0.2652 76.0% 2.6%
0.5452 68.2% 4.9%
1.0000 0.0% 0.0%

The last row is the control: when the pool is the corpus, both frames are the same set by construction and the hidden fraction is zero. The effect is also statistic-dependent — 7 bigram units against 35 word-3 units at the same threshold — which becomes the whole story two sections down.

The misclassification is a function of who is writing

Put the guard on a five-language corpus (7,521 documents: 3,200 English, 1,354 Italian, 1,767 Spanish, 800 French, 400 German) and plant a register: a recurring block a community shares — a greeting, a header, a template clause — carried by a fraction phi of that community's documents. Its corpus prevalence is s * phi, so the prevalence at which a corpus-wide frame becomes able to remove it is

phi* = theta / s

At word3, tau = 0.5, theta = 0.05, with the Italian community as the smaller stratum (share 0.180) and English as the larger (0.425):

register prevalence φ Italian: corpus-frame fires English: corpus-frame fires
0.00 0 / 120 0 / 120
0.05 120 / 120 16 / 120
0.20 107 / 120 0 / 120
0.50 0 / 120 0 / 120
1.00 0 / 120 0 / 120

The community-level frame fires 0 of 120 in every one of those cells. So the same register, at the same prevalence, is missed entirely in the minority community and caught entirely in the majority — and the reason is arithmetic, not tuning. At phi = 0.20 the register's corpus prevalence is 0.036 in the Italian community (hidden, 107 pairs of fires induced) and 0.085 in English (visible, 0 induced).

The critical prevalence is measured by bracketing, not assumed: the Italian community flips between a prevalence at which the register is hidden and one at which it is visible, bracketing the predicted 0.278; English brackets 0.118. The prediction is checked exactly against theta / s in all twelve (statistic × stratum × threshold) rows of the artefact, which is what you would expect from an identity and would not from a fit.

That is what makes a mis-set frame a fairness defect rather than a tuning knob: the band of blindness (0, phi*) is wider for the smaller community, so the filter silently protects the majority's boilerplate and quietly flags the minority's.

The statistic decides whether your community has a stratum at all

The certificate s * phi < theta <=> register hidden from the corpus frame holds in 48 of 48 word-3 cells. On character bigrams it fails in all 48 — 0 of 48 predicted-hidden cells are actually hidden.

That failure is not a defect, it is the premise: character bigrams recur across languages, so they are not confined to a community, so their corpus frequency does not dilute, so they stay inside the corpus frame at any share. An analyst who picks the statistic is picking whether their community is visible at all — and nothing in the API of a dedup pipeline tells them they made that choice.

Two controls keep this from being "everything is a level effect". A verbatim repost and a 1%-edited repost (Dice 0.990) must fire under every level including the corpus frame; both fire in all three threshold cells. The level cannot remove a genuine copy — which is exactly what separates a register effect from a similarity effect.

The residue threshold has a boundary, and the zero above it is derived

Widen the grid to 1,980 cells (2 strata × 2 statistics × 6 prevalences × 3 frame thresholds × 3 similarity thresholds × 5 residue thresholds × 2 sampling rules) and sweep r.

The level-induced count (corpus-frame fires minus community-frame fires) is flat for every r from 5 to 27 — 108 induced fires at r = 5 and 108 at r = 27 — then drops to 0 at r = 40. The instrument explains the zero rather than reporting it: at that prevalence the corpus residue over the eligible pairs never exceeds 28 units while the community residue never exceeds 1, so at r = 40 the corpus level cannot fire on any pair, even though 108 of them pass the similarity gate.

Which gives a design boundary rather than a small measurement: the residue threshold has to be <= register_units for a community register to be able to decide it at all. The grid charges its own certificate over the 198 cells where r exceeds the register's size, and requires the induced count to be zero there. It is: all 198, zero.

A rate is owed over its eligible subset

Here is the mistake I had to fix in my own table before publishing it. A pair whose similarity gate does not open is ineligible, not unflagged. Counting it divides the rate by the pass fraction and deflates the effect — silently, in a direction that makes the filter look better than it is.

Same effect, two sampling rules:

sampling eligible pairs level-induced fires eligible rate dilution
affected (both members carry the register) 120 108 1.000 0.900
community (random pairs of the community) 3 3 1.000 0.025

The two rates agree and the counts differ only by the dilution, which is why both numbers belong in the same table. And an empty denominator is written undef, never plotted as 0.000 — a zero you reached by having no data is not a zero you measured.

The null is a level too

The last instrument plants ground truth by construction: 4,763 documents, 24 verbatim reposts (hash-equal after normalisation) and 12 edited reposts at a declared 0.02 character substitution rate. Three laws, each with a certificate.

L1 — a filter chain is a sensitivity curve, not a point. An expectation computed as N_eligible * P_null is a product of two measured rates, and the identity E_matched / E_naive = (N_eligible / N_raw) * P_null is asserted exactly — measured 0.9995 on this corpus (36.98 against 37), i.e. the two routes coincide to four decimals. Now de-generic-filter only the scan and not its null, and the expectation inflates by an amount that depends entirely on where you set the rule:

de-generic threshold (units) inflation
10 1.00×
25 1.40×
50 3.88×
100 16.68×

On long documents the loosest rule is a near no-op (null survivor rate 0.9995), so the honest reading is: the mechanism is real and its magnitude is a function of the threshold and of your document-length profile.

L2 — an interval belongs to the population it resampled. A bootstrap over the whole fire population (37 fires, of which 25 are verbatim and identical by hash) gives the degenerate [1.0, 1.0]. The 12 non-identical fires give [0.739, 0.880], median 0.788. interval_transfers = False: the wider interval cannot be read off the whole-ensemble resample, because the subset was carved out after the resample. A count that small also owns a count-based bound and not a distributional one — Poisson 95% upper 19.4 one-sided, 21.0 two-sided, for k = 12 — and which convention you used is part of the number.

L3 — the null's population is the pairing, not only the marginals. Each cell is the fraction of reference scores strictly below their own null's median, so a calibrated null reads 0.5:

set anchored null exchangeable null marginal null
control (cross-language, matched-length, unrelated; 150 pairs) 0.487 0.460 0.587
near-duplicates (37 pairs) 0.000 0.324 0.000

Reproducing the two length marginals is therefore not reproducing the pair's joint: the variable a marginal null frees is the pairing itself. And on the near-duplicate set, a null drawn from a pool that contains the near-duplicates inflates the reference's apparent surprise — 0.324 instead of 0.000 — which is the same "population decides the null" mechanism one layer down.

The --selftest plants a deliberately biased null that must not read 0.5, so the calibration check fires on its own fault rather than passing by construction.

If you maintain one of these filters

Four things transfer, and none of them require my corpus:

  1. State the level of your background frame, and compute it at the level you care about. A global frame protects the majority's boilerplate. If your users are communities of unequal size, the smaller one's shared units are below your threshold by construction.
  2. Know whether your units are confined. Word n-grams and phrases dilute with community share; character n-grams usually do not. That choice decides whether a community stratum exists at all in your data.
  3. Check r against the size of the boilerplate you care about. If your residue threshold exceeds a template's unit count, no template can ever be the thing that decides a flag — the check is decorative for that class of input.
  4. Report rates over eligible pairs, and read your null off the pairing. Both are places where a number that looks correct is measuring the denominator instead of the effect.

The full package — four instruments, a pinned corpus with its own SHA256SUMS, seven figures, a 135-entry reference gate and a one-command reproduction that re-renders the manuscript byte-identically — is at silicon-science-cs / issue #132. The reproduction runs in about ten seconds and refuses to measure a corpus whose checksums do not verify.

articles.title: A bunch of Vibe Coding idiosyncrasies to beginners
articles.description: Do you know vibe coding?    Before you answer, please open 20 PRs with AI, get burned at least once,...
articles.body_html:
Do you know vibe coding?

Before you answer, please open 20 PRs with AI, get burned at least once, and only then come back.

Please share this with friends who just discovered Cursor / Claude / Grok.

¯\(ツ)/¯

This is a collection of things that happen when you vibe code that may not be well recognized, especially to beginners.

Disclaimer: Some of these are simply to demonstrate the quirky parts of AI-assisted coding and by no means encourage best practices.

Q. What's the result?

You: "Add a login form"
AI: *generates a full Next.js app with auth, middleware, database, and tests*

A.

You now have 47 files you didn't ask for and a bug in the middleware.

Q. What's the result?

You: "Fix this function"
AI: *rewrites the entire file*

A.

Your git diff is now unreadable and you lost the one comment that explained the weird edge case.

Q. What's the result?

You: "Use the official SDK"
AI: import { Client } from 'super-cool-sdk-that-does-not-exist'

A.

npm install fails. The package never existed. The AI was very confident.

Q. What's the result?

You paste 3 files into the chat.
You: "Why is this failing?"
AI: *gives a perfect answer based on only the first file*

A.

The real bug was in file 3. The AI never saw it.

Q. What's the result?

You: "Make it faster"
AI: *adds caching, memoization, web workers, and a Redis layer*

A.

Your 20ms function is now 40ms and has a new dependency.

Q. What's the result?

You: "This code works in the playground"
*paste it into your project*

A.

It doesn't work. Missing imports, wrong types, and it assumed global variables that don't exist.

Q. What's the result?

You ask Claude, Grok, and ChatGPT the same question.

A.

Three different answers. All of them sound correct. One of them is.

Q. What's the result?

You: "Don't change the function signature"
AI: *changes the function signature*

A.

It also updated the call sites. Half of them are wrong.

Q. What's the result?

You: "Explain this error"
AI: "This is a common issue with async/await"

A.

The error was a missing comma. The AI never looked at the actual stack trace.

Q. What's the result?

You accept every suggestion for 2 hours.

A.

Your codebase now has 4 different ways to do the same thing and you can't explain any of them.

Q. What's the result?

You: "Write tests"
AI: *writes tests that pass*

A.

The tests test the AI's implementation, not your requirements. They will pass even when the feature is broken.

Q. What's the result?

You: "Just a small change"
AI: *refactors half the module "for clarity"*

A.

The small change is correct. The refactor introduced two new bugs.

Q. What's the result?

You: "Use the latest version of X"
AI: *uses a version from 2023*

A.

The API it used was removed last year. The AI was very confident.

Q. What's the result?

You copy AI code into production.

A.

It works until the edge case the AI never considered. Then you spend the next hour debugging code you don't understand.

Q. What's the result?

You: "Make it production ready"
AI: *adds logging, error handling, retries, and metrics*

A.

Your prototype is now 300 lines longer and still missing the one validation you actually needed.

Q. What's the result?

You ask the AI to review its own code.

A.

It finds two style issues and misses the logic bug.

Q. What's the result?

You: "Don't use any libraries"
AI: *uses three*

A.

One of them is unmaintained.

Q. What's the result?

You regenerate the same component five times.

A.

You now have five slightly different versions and no idea which one is correct.

Q. What's the result?

You: "This is taking too long, just ship it"

A.

You ship it. The bug shows up in production on Friday at 5pm.

Q. What's the result?

You finally read the code the AI wrote.

A.

You understand it less than when you started.

Released under the "I should have just written it myself" license.

articles.title: Don't Let the LLM Decide: How I Built a Predictable AI Tutor
articles.description: The easy way to build an AI tutor is to give the LLM everything. Pass it the question, the learner's...
articles.body_html:
The easy way to build an AI tutor is to give the LLM everything. Pass it the question, the learner's attempts and the answer. Tell it: "Help the learner, but don't give the answer away too early."

That works in a demo. It fails in an experiment. And it fails quietly in production too.

In the first post of this series I explained the experiment. I built an SQL tutor in two versions, called arms. Arm A makes you try before it helps, then gives a hint before the answer. Arm B gives the answer whenever you ask, like most AI tools. Six people used one or the other, then took a test a week later with no tutor.

This post is about how I built it. The core rule fits on one line:

The LLM never decides whether to help, or how much. Plain code decides. The LLM only writes the hint's wording, after that decision is made.

Why the LLM can't be the one deciding

Picture the prompt version. "If the learner seems stuck, give a hint. If they've really tried, give the answer."

Now try to answer one question: what did Arm A receive?

You can't. "Seems stuck" is a judgment the model makes fresh every time. Two learners in the same situation can get different help. The same learner can get different help on a retry. The thing you're trying to test becomes a moving target.

There's a second problem. With six people, there were only about 23 moments in the whole study where the tutor had to decide what help to give. You can't judge a model's decision-making from 23 examples. But you can fully test a plain function, and I did, with 123 unit tests.

So I split the system into three kinds of parts, a framing from my 100x Engineers AI course:

part does what why it sits there
human writes and runs SQL the skill being measured is theirs
deterministic (plain code) the try-first rule, the hint/answer rules, the answer checker, the leak guard the one thing being tested must be fixed and checkable
probabilistic (the LLM) writes the hint text, nothing else prose about this specific mistake is the one thing code can't write

The model is one small component. It's not the product.

The policy: a pure function

Here's the heart of policy.js, trimmed. No DOM, no network, no LLM. It takes the log for one question and returns an action.

const ACTION = {
  NONE:         'none',          // already solved
  REFUSE_GATE:  'refuse_gate',   // Arm A, no real attempt yet
  REFUSE_RETRY: 'refuse_retry',  // Arm A, hint given, keep trying
  HINT:         'hint',          // the LLM writes the text
  REVEAL:       'reveal',        // the reference query
};

const DEFAULT_N = 2; // attempts with the hint before the answer

function decide(item) {
  const N = item.N ?? DEFAULT_N;
  const counted = countableAttempts(item.attempts);
  const helpServed = item.helpServed || [];

  if (item.attempts.some(a => a.outcome === 'correct')) return { action: ACTION.NONE };

  // Arm B: the entire difference between the two groups is this line.
  if (item.arm === 'B') return { action: ACTION.REVEAL };

  // Arm A: the gate. No help of any kind until one attempt counts.
  if (counted.length === 0) return { action: ACTION.REFUSE_GATE };

  if (helpServed.some(h => h.action === ACTION.REVEAL)) return { action: ACTION.REVEAL };

  const hint = helpServed.find(h => h.action === ACTION.HINT);
  if (!hint) return { action: ACTION.HINT };

  const sinceHint = counted.length - hint.afterCountedAttempts;
  return sinceHint >= N ? { action: ACTION.REVEAL } : { action: ACTION.REFUSE_RETRY };
}

The only thing of interest here is the Arm B line. That one if is the whole difference between the two versions. Anyone can read it and know exactly what each group got.

Every decision is logged with counted and sinceHint. So for any Help press, I can look at the log and prove why the tutor responded the way it did.

N is fixed at 2 for everyone. If it changed per person, I'd be testing two things at once, and three people per group can't separate them.

What counts as an attempt?

Arm A's rule is "try first". I call it the gate: no help until you've made an attempt. So the code needs to decide what a real attempt is. This turned out to be the hardest part of the policy.

My first version said: an attempt counts if its result set is different from the last one. Simple, and wrong.

The bug: a query that doesn't run has no result set. So for a learner who couldn't get anything to execute, no attempt ever counted. The gate never opened. In my earlier test rounds, 101 of 122 attempts had a syntax error and didn't run. This wasn't an edge case. It was the main case.

And a query that fails to parse can still carry a full, wrong mental model:

SELECT customer, COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE COUNT(*) > 3

That doesn't run. It's also a perfect example of the exact mistake I was teaching about (filtering groups with WHERE instead of HAVING). It should count.

But asdf doesn't parse either. If junk counts, a learner can type three bits of junk and get a hint while thinking about nothing. Research on tutoring systems calls this "gaming the system", and learners find that shortcut fast.

So I added a substance bar. An attempt must contain one SQL keyword and one name from this question's schema:

function isSubstantive(sql, identifiers) {
  const low = String(sql ?? '').toLowerCase();
  if (!low.trim()) return false;
  if (!SQL_KEYWORDS.some(k => low.includes(k))) return false;
  if (!identifiers.length) return true; // fail open, see below
  return identifiers.some(id =>
    id.length >= 4
      ? low.includes(id)
      : new RegExp(`\\b${id}\\b`).test(low) // so "id" doesn't match "video"
  );
}

Matching is by substring on purpose. Real learners wrote GroupBy and havingcount>=3. That's mangled spelling, but a real mental model. A strict token match would throw those away.

I checked it against all 128 attempts from the screening round. 121 passed. The 7 rejected were 6 empty submissions and one bare SELECT. No real attempt was lost.

Notice the fail open line. If the schema list fails to load, the bar only checks for a keyword. A misconfigured page must not silently refuse every learner. That would turn Arm A into "no help at all" without anyone noticing.

The leak guard

Here's the uncomfortable part. To write a useful hint about a wrong query, the LLM has to see the correct one. I call that the reference query. So it's holding the answer while it writes. Sometimes it just prints it.

If that reaches the learner, Arm A quietly becomes Arm B on that question. The experiment stops testing anything, and nothing in the logs looks wrong.

So every hint passes through hint-guard.js before the learner sees it. It's deterministic. It makes no model calls. It looks at text and says yes or no.

function inspect(hint, { referenceQuery, learnerQuery }) {
  // 1. A runnable query: SELECT plus a real table after FROM/JOIN.
  // 2. A clause that distinguishes the reference query,
  //    unless the learner already wrote it themselves.
  // 3. Too much of the reference reproduced word for word.
  // 4. A walkthrough: four or more SQL keywords named.
}

If a hint is rejected, the system asks the model once more. If that fails too, it serves a hand-written fallback for that question. Every attempt and every rejection is logged.

Results: on 101 real hints, zero false alarms. Against 24 leaks I wrote specifically to beat it, it caught 22.

What can go wrong

Each rule in the guard exists because an earlier, simpler rule broke.

"SELECT and FROM means a leak." My first check rejected any hint containing both words. But they're normal English. "You started with SELECT, but where does the data come FROM?" is a great hint, and it got blocked. The fix: a runnable query must name a real table. The reference query tells you which tables exist, so look for those.

The semicolon rule. I also rejected "select ... ;" on the idea that a semicolon ends a statement. English uses semicolons too. "Nothing is processed; you need to say where the data comes from" got blocked. I deleted that rule instead of patching it, because the table rule already covered real queries.

Quoting the learner back to themselves. The prompt asks the model to quote what the learner wrote. So a hint would say "your MAX(price) is fine". MAX(price) is part of the answer, so the guard blocked it. 7 of 8 rejections in one test run were this. But the learner already wrote it. It's in their editor. Now a clause only counts as a leak if the learner doesn't already have it.

The leak with no SQL in it. "The FROM keyword picks the products table, then GROUP BY groups the rows by category..." No clause appears verbatim, but you could type the answer straight from it. The signal is shape, not content. A real hint talks about one or two things. A dictation names everything.

I didn't pick the threshold by feel. I measured it. Across the 101 real hints: 66 named no SQL keyword, 29 named one, 5 named two, 1 named three, and none named four. The two prose leaks named six and seven. A limit of four separates them with room on both sides.

The silent fallback. The LLM sits behind a Supabase edge function, so the API key never reaches the browser. Supabase pauses free projects after about a week without traffic. When paused, nothing errors. Arm A just serves the hand-written backup hints. The app looks fine, but it's quietly running a different tutor. I found this once, fixed it, and added a script to check it before every session.

What this means for your code

If you're putting an LLM into a product, ask one question about each decision: does this need judgment, or does it need to be the same every time?

  • If the behaviour has to be explainable, testable or consistent, it belongs in code.
  • If it needs language about this specific case, that's what the model is for.
  • Put a deterministic check between the model and the user for anything that would be expensive if the model got it wrong.

In my tutor, that split is why I could say exactly what each group got. It's also why the experiment could fail honestly. When two of my checks failed, I knew the failure was about learners, not about a model behaving differently on a Tuesday.

Next in the series: the mistakes I made running my first controlled experiment as a developer, including the one a Demo Day judge caught.

vikrantnegi / withholding-pilot

Learning OS — 100x Cohort 7 final capstone

Vikrant Negi. Solo. Demo Day track. Submission 7 Oct 2026.

An SQL tutor that makes you try before it helps, and a 6-person pilot testing whether that changes what you can do a week later, with the tutor gone.

For where things stand today, read STATUS.md. That is the only file that claims to be current.

  • ?arm=B opens the baseline. Help gives the full answer at once.
