articles.title: How a power station runtime estimate is computed (and why it rounds down)
articles.description: A portable power station says "1,000 Wh" on the box, but nobody gets 1,000 Wh of AC output from it....
articles.body_html:
A portable power station says "1,000 Wh" on the box, but nobody gets 1,000 Wh of AC output from it. While building a runtime calculator, I had to decide how to turn a spec sheet into a number people can plan around. Here is the model I ended up with, and why every choice leans conservative.

The core idea: subtract losses, then divide

Runtime is just energy divided by power. The work is in being honest about both sides of that division.

Energy side. The rated watt-hours are measured at the cell level. You can't pull all of it out: the battery management system stops discharge before the cells are truly empty. I default to using 90% of rated capacity.

Power side. If your load is an AC device, the inverter has to convert DC from the battery. Inverters aren't perfect, so I assume 88% efficiency. The inverter also burns power just by being switched on, even with nothing plugged in. I assume a 10 W idle draw and add it to the load.

The formula 

function runtimeHours({ ratedWh, loadW, usableShare = 0.9, inverterEff = 0.88, idleW = 10 }) {
  const usableWh = ratedWh * usableShare;
  const drawW = loadW / inverterEff + idleW;   // what the battery really supplies
  return Math.floor((usableWh / drawW) * 10) / 10; // always round down
}

runtimeHours({ ratedWh: 1000, loadW: 100 }); // 7.2 h, not 10 h

For a 100 W load on a 1,000 Wh unit: usable energy is 900 Wh, the battery supplies about 123.6 W (100 / 0.88 + 10), so you get 7.28 hours, which floors to 7.2. It is nowhere near the 10 hours the naive division suggests.

Fridges are not constant loads

A fridge's nameplate wattage is what it draws while the compressor runs. The compressor cycles, so over a day it runs about a third of the time. I model that as a duty cycle of roughly 33%:

const fridgeAvgW = fridgeRunningW * 0.33;

Treating a 150 W fridge as a constant 150 W would underestimate runtime by a factor of three. Treating it as 50 W forever ignores startup surge, which is a separate check on whether the inverter can start the compressor at all.

One number is a lie, so show a range

Real conditions vary: temperature, battery age, how hard devices actually pull. Instead of a single figure I output three:

  • Cautious: pushes the assumptions the wrong way (lower usable share, lower efficiency, higher idle draw).
  • Typical: the defaults above.
  • Optimistic: assumptions nudged the other way. 
const scenarios = {
  cautious:   { usableShare: 0.85, inverterEff: 0.85, idleW: 15 },
  typical:    { usableShare: 0.90, inverterEff: 0.88, idleW: 10 },
  optimistic: { usableShare: 0.95, inverterEff: 0.92, idleW: 8 },
};

The spread is the useful part. If the cautious case still covers your outage, you're fine. If only the optimistic one does, you know to buy more capacity or cut loads.

Why always round down

Rounding a runtime up by even half an hour can mean a CPAP machine or a router dies at 3 a.m. Rounding down costs the user nothing but a little pessimism. I apply Math.floor at the very last step, never in the middle of the calculation, so errors don't compound.

Things I deliberately don't do

  • I don't invent numbers. If a manufacturer doesn't publish a spec, the field stays empty rather than being guessed.
  • I don't hide defaults. Every assumption is printed next to the result so you can disagree with it.

Try it

I put this model into a free calculator, Kilohour, so you can check the math against your own devices. If you think any default is off, I'd like to hear which one and why. These are defaults, not laws of physics, and measured data from real units would improve them.

articles.title: Rename the Variable, Change the Security Verdict
articles.description: One of my own rules flags a Zod schema containing no XPath, and stays silent on textbook XPath injection. Both come from the same heuristic: it decides whether a value is attacker-controlled by substring-matching the variable's name.
articles.body_html:
Four lines, run through my own XPath injection rule today:

xpath.select("//user[@id='" + id     + "']", doc);   // silent
xpath.select("//user[@id='" + userId + "']", doc);   // FIRES

export const QueryValidateSchema = QueryInputSchema; // FIRES
export const SchemaA             = SchemaB;          // silent

The first two are the same vulnerability. The last two are the same statement.
The only thing that changed is what the variables are called.

The heuristic

no-xpath-injection has to decide whether a value is attacker-controlled. Here
is how it decides:

const varName = inputNode.name.toLowerCase();
if (["req", "request", "query", "params", "input", "user", "search"]
      .some((keyword) => varName.includes(keyword))) {
  return true;   // tainted
}

That is the whole test. Not where the value came from — what it is spelled.

Both errors, one cause

The false positive. QueryInputSchema lowercases to queryinputschema,
which contains query and also input. Tainted. There is no XPath call in
that statement at all — it is a Zod schema being re-exported. The rule reports
an injection risk on an assignment.

The false negative. id contains none of the seven substrings, so the
value is not tainted, so a concatenation flowing into xpath.select — a sink
this rule already recognises, it is in the default xpathFunctions list — is
not reported. Textbook XPath injection, silently accepted.

The //user[...] string does contain user. It does not matter: the check
runs on the identifier, never on the literal.

One predicate, opposite failures. That is what makes this a single defect
rather than two bugs that happen to share a file.

Why this is worse than being wrong

A rule with a 70% false-positive rate is annoying and legible — you read the
findings, you see the noise, you tune it or drop it.

This is not that. This rule is right about the shape of the problem and
wrong about the input to it, which means its errors correlate with naming
conventions rather than with code. A codebase that says userInput gets
flagged everywhere. A codebase that says val, x, raw or id gets a clean
report and the same vulnerabilities.

Two teams, identical risk, opposite verdicts — and neither has any way to tell
from the output which one they are.

It also fails toward silence in exactly the case that matters. Short, neutral
identifiers are what you find in the compact, clever code most likely to be
doing something sharp with strings.

What it should read instead

The value's origin, not its spelling. Did it come from a request handler
parameter, a process.argv, a req.* member, a function boundary the rule
cannot see past? That is
taint analysis,
and it is more expensive than a substring match — which is precisely why the
substring match was written.

The honest framing is that this rule is a heuristic wearing a taint rule's
messaging. The fix is not a longer keyword list. A longer list moves the
boundary; it does not stop the verdict being a function of names.

The check that finds these

Take any rule you rely on. Write the vulnerable case. Then rename every
identifier in it to a single letter and run it again.

If the verdict changes, the rule is reading names. You now know something about
your tooling that no amount of reading its findings would have told you —
because a finding you never get is indistinguishable from a clean file, and
precision and recall measured on a corpus that shares your naming conventions will both look fine.
It is the same reason a labelled fixture set catches what unit tests miss:
the tests assert the rule's behaviour on the names its author chose.

This is a known class in our own tracker, with a lint check that gates new
occurrences and a documented list of the ones still outstanding. This rule is
on that list. Measured against the workspace build of
eslint-plugin-secure-coding
today — if you are on the published release, re-run before assuming.

The rule is
no-xpath-injection;
the predicate is in
its source.
Both are open, which is the only reason this article can be specific.

⭐ Star the repo if you would rather find your linter's blind spots in an article than in an incident.

eslint-plugin-secure-coding is part of the Interlace ESLint ecosystem. Source on GitHub · Follow: Dev.to/ofri-peretz

Rename the variables in your worst file to single letters. Does your linter still find the bug?

articles.title: A financial calculator is only as good as its formula
articles.description: Online financial calculators have a trust problem. You type in your numbers, a monthly payment...
articles.body_html:
Online financial calculators have a trust problem. You type in your numbers, a monthly payment appears, and you have no idea what math produced it. Was that mortgage calc using monthly or semi-annual compounding? Does the tax calculator include state tax? Which year's brackets? Usually, you can't tell — the formula is hidden.

I think the fix is embarrassingly simple: publish the formula. Here's what that looks like in practice, from building a set of financial calculators.

Show the math on the page

Every calculator should display the actual formula it uses, with the variables labeled. For compound interest, that's A = P(1 + r/n)^(nt) — and then define each symbol in plain language. This does two things: users can verify the result by hand, and other developers can spot your mistakes. Both have happened to me, and both made the tool better.

State your assumptions explicitly

A mortgage calculator isn't just a formula — it's a stack of assumptions: compounding frequency, whether property tax and insurance are included, how extra payments are applied. List them next to the result. The calculators people trust most are the ones that say "here's what I assumed" instead of pretending there's one true answer.

Run it client-side

Financial numbers are sensitive. Running the calculation entirely in the browser means the numbers never leave the user's device — there's no server log of someone's salary or mortgage balance to leak. As a bonus, results update instantly as you type, which makes the tool feel dramatically better.

Test against known values

Before shipping, verify each calculator against authoritative sources: IRS tax tables for the income tax calc, bank-published amortization examples for mortgages. Write these as actual test cases, not eyeball checks. One wrong assumption in a refinance calculator can cost a real person real money.

Write guides, not just inputs

Most people don't know what "points" or "PMI" mean. A short plain-English explanation next to each input turns a calculator from a black box into a learning tool — and it's what separates a useful page from a commodity widget.

I applied all of this building CalcWise (https://finance.toppn.com/) — 9 free financial calculators covering compound interest, mortgage, refinance, credit-card payoff, retirement, investing, income tax, ROI and profit margin. Formulas published, everything runs locally in the browser, no sign-up. The most valuable feedback I've gotten wasn't feature requests — it was people checking my math. That's exactly the dynamic you want.

articles.title: Your 'Expand All' Button Is Quietly Causing Layout Thrashing
articles.description: An 'expand all' click that stutters isn't a slow CPU — it's layout thrashing, a loop that forces the browser to recalculate layout once per row instead of once per click. Here's how to spot it and the two-line fix.
articles.body_html:
You click "Expand all" on a settings page or an FAQ list, and for a moment, nothing happens. Not nothing-nothing — the click registered, the network tab is quiet, there's no spinner. The page is just... stuck, for a beat, before every row snaps open at once.

Nobody wrote a slow function on purpose. The code probably looks completely reasonable. That's what makes this one worth knowing: the bug isn't in what the loop does, it's in the order it does it in.

The loop that looks fine

Here's a version of the handler almost everyone writes the first time:

function expandAll(rows) {
  rows.forEach((row) => {
    const content = row.querySelector(".row-content");
    const height = content.scrollHeight; // read
    content.style.height = height + "px"; // write
  });
}

Read the current content height, set the element to that height so the height: 0 → height: auto-style expand animation has something to animate toward. Repeat for every row. It's clean, it's obviously correct, and it ships.

Open your browser's performance profiler, click "Expand all" on a list of forty or fifty rows, and record. You'll see a stack of narrow purple bars, one per row, each labeled something like "Forced reflow" or "Forced synchronous layout". That label is the browser telling you exactly what just happened, in its own words.

Why reading a height can be slow

Browsers don't recompute layout after every style change. They batch it — style and layout writes pile up in a queue, and the engine runs one layout pass right before the next paint. That's why setting ten CSS properties in a row usually costs about the same as setting one.

But some reads break the batch. scrollHeight, offsetHeight, offsetWidth, clientWidth, getBoundingClientRect(), getComputedStyle() — anything that hands you back a real number has to be correct right now, not "correct as of the last paint." If there's a pending style write the browser hasn't applied to layout yet, it can't answer honestly without doing the work first. So it does the work first: it flushes every queued change and recalculates layout, synchronously, on the spot, then hands you the number.

Now look at the loop again. Each iteration writes content.style.height, which invalidates layout. The next iteration reads scrollHeight on a different element — but the browser doesn't know your next read doesn't care about the previous write, so it has to flush and recalculate to be sure. Forty rows means forty forced layouts, each one touching the whole document, not just the row you're looking at. That's layout thrashing: alternating reads and writes that force the same work the browser was trying to batch away, over and over, inside a single click handler, on the main thread, blocking everything else — including the next frame.

The fix is reordering, not rewriting

You don't need a library for this. You need two loops instead of one:

function expandAll(rows) {
  const contents = rows.map((row) => row.querySelector(".row-content"));

  // 1. read every height first — one flush, if any, covers all of them
  const heights = contents.map((c) => c.scrollHeight);

  // 2. write every height second — no reads in between to force a recalculation
  contents.forEach((c, i) => {
    c.style.height = heights[i] + "px";
  });
}

Same inputs, same visual result, same number of DOM nodes touched. The only change is that every read happens before every write. The browser still has to recalculate layout once, to answer the first scrollHeight honestly — but after that, it's just queuing style changes, which it was always good at batching. One forced layout instead of N.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

This is the whole idea behind the old "FastDOM" pattern, and it's worth internalizing as a rule rather than a library: never interleave a layout read with a layout write inside a loop. Batch the reads, batch the writes, in that order.

Where this hides in real code

It's rarely written as nakedly as the example above. It shows up as:

  • A ResizeObserver or scroll handler that reads getBoundingClientRect() on one element, then immediately updates another element's size based on it, inside a loop over a list.
  • A virtualized list or masonry layout that measures each item's height to position the next one — read, position, read, position.
  • An animation library (or a hand-rolled one) that reads the current transform of an element to compute the next frame's value, for every animated element, every frame.

The common shape is always "measure, then move, then measure the next thing" — and the fix is always the same two passes: measure everything, then move everything.

If you're not sure whether your own code does this, the profiler will tell you faster than reading the source will. Record a trace around the interaction you suspect, and search for "Forced reflow" in the summary. If it's there, it names the exact call stack that triggered it — you don't have to guess.

What this costs you, and what it doesn't

This isn't a feature flag or a browser quirk you need to check support tables for — every layout engine works this way, because batching writes and flushing on-demand reads is the only way to be both fast in the common case and correct when a script actually needs a real number. There's nothing to polyfill and nothing to feature-detect. The fix costs you an array and a second loop, which is a rounding error next to the forced layouts it removes.

What it does cost you is a bit of discipline: every time you write a loop that both measures and changes the DOM, ask which one happens first, and whether it happens for every item before the loop moves to the next. One extra array, two passes instead of one — that's the entire price of not blocking your own main thread on your own click handler.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

Next time a click handler stutters and the network tab is empty, open the performance panel before you reach for a spinner or a setTimeout. What's the slowest "obviously fine" loop you've found hiding a forced reflow? I'd genuinely like to know — drop it in the comments.

articles.title: The 'vibe coding' bubble has a rendering problem nobody is talking about
articles.description: Vibe coding is the dominant trend in web development in 2026. You type a prompt, get a working app in...
articles.body_html:
Vibe coding is the dominant trend in web development in 2026. You type a prompt, get a working app in 30 seconds, and ship it. Lovable, Bolt, v0, and similar tools have made it possible to prototype and deploy a web application without writing a line of code.

The apps look good. They work in a browser. They are invisible to AI search engines.

The problem

Every tool in the vibe coding stack produces a client-side rendered SPA by default. The server returns an HTML shell with a <div id="root"></div> and a <script> tag. The browser downloads the script, executes it, and renders the content. In a browser, this works. For a bot, it does not.

GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot, and Googlebot do not execute JavaScript the way a browser does. They fetch the HTML, parse it, and move on. If the content is not in the HTML, it does not exist for the retrieval pipeline.

This is not a new problem. It is the same rendering problem that has plagued SPAs since React popularized client-side rendering. What is new is the scale. In 2026, tens of thousands of sites are being generated by vibe coding tools, and every one of them ships with the same default: empty HTML shell, JavaScript-rendered content, invisible to crawlers.

How to check 

curl -s https://your-vibe-coded-site.com | wc -c

If the response is a few hundred bytes, you are getting the shell. If it is several kilobytes or more, the content is in the HTML.

You can also check what a bot sees by looking at the page source, not the rendered DOM:

curl -s https://your-vibe-coded-site.com | grep -i "your main content text"

If the grep returns nothing, your content is JavaScript-rendered. No AI search engine can read it.

Why llms.txt does not fix this

The llms.txt debate has consumed the GEO conversation for months. Google says to ignore it. Chrome Lighthouse audits for it. Four independent studies say it has no effect on AI citations (see the first article in this series for the full data).

But even if llms.txt worked perfectly, it would not fix the rendering problem. An llms.txt file links to your pages. When an AI bot follows those links, it fetches your HTML. If your HTML is empty, the bot reads the file, visits the pages, and finds nothing. The file is a map to empty rooms.

The Ahrefs study confirmed this pattern: AI bots fetch HTML pages, not auxiliary files. The Limy study tracked 515 million bot events and found that bots overwhelmingly request HTML directly. The retrieval step that decides what to cite reads your HTML. If your HTML has no content, you are invisible.

The fix

The fix is not AI-specific. It is the same fix that has existed since SPAs became popular:

Option 1: Static generation. Generate complete HTML at build time. Astro, Next.js with output: export, Gatsby, and Elevento do this by default. Every page is a full HTML file. Bots get everything on the first request.

Option 2: Server-side rendering. Render HTML on the server for each request. Next.js with App Router, Nuxt, and SvelteKit support this. The server sends complete HTML. Bots can read it.

Option 3: Prerendering. Generate static snapshots of your pages and serve them to bots. This is a workaround that adds complexity and can be flagged as cloaking if the prerendered content differs from what users see. Avoid it unless you have no other option.

What the vibe coding tools should do

The tools that generate SPAs should default to static generation or SSR. Right now, they default to CSR because it is the simplest path to a working prototype. The user types a prompt, the tool generates a React app, and the app works in the browser. The fact that it is invisible to crawlers is not visible to the user until they check their analytics and wonder why they have zero organic traffic.

Some tools are starting to address this. Lovable has added an SSR option. Bolt supports deployment to platforms that handle prerendering. But the defaults still favor CSR, and most users do not change defaults.

The broader implication

The rendering problem is the base layer of AI search visibility. If your content is not in your HTML, nothing else matters. Not llms.txt, not Schema, not content structure, not citation-worthy passages. The bot has to be able to read your page before any of the higher-level signals can work.

In the audit tool I maintain, geo-optimizer-skill, the rendering check is the first signal we test. We fetch the page with and without a headless browser and compare the results. If the content differs significantly, we flag it as JS-dependent. This is the most common failure mode we see, and it is the one with the clearest fix.

If you are vibe coding, check your HTML output. If it is empty, switch to SSG or SSR. Your app will look the same to users and become visible to every search engine and AI crawler that matters. The fix is one configuration change, not a GEO strategy.

articles.title: Sending transactional email from Node.js in Ghana (and paying with mobile money)
articles.description: Every app eventually needs to send email: a sign-up confirmation, a password reset, a receipt. The...
articles.body_html:
Every app eventually needs to send email: a sign-up confirmation, a password reset, a receipt. The usual answer is SendGrid, Mailgun or Resend, and they're good services. But if you're building in Ghana, you hit the same wall I did: they're priced in dollars and want an international card.

So I built Sankofa, an email API that's prepaid in cedis. You top up with MTN MoMo, Telecel Cash or AirtelTigo Money at GHS 5 per 1,000 emails, with no subscription.

This post walks through sending email from a Node.js app with it, from your first test email to bulk sends and delivery webhooks.

1. Get an API key

Create an account, then open API Keys in the dashboard and create one. It starts with esk_ and is shown once, so put it straight into your environment:

export SANKOFA_API_KEY=esk_your_api_key

Keep it on your server. Never put it in frontend code, where anyone can read it.

2. Send your first email (no DNS needed)

Normally you can't send email until you've verified a domain. To get you going sooner, every account can use a shared test sender, hello@test.trysankofa.com, which can only send to the email address you signed up with:

const response = await fetch("https://api.trysankofa.com/v1/emails", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANKOFA_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: "hello@test.trysankofa.com",
    to: "you@example.com", // the address you signed up with
    subject: "Hello from my app",
    text: "It works!",
  }),
});

const body = await response.json();
if (!response.ok) throw new Error(`${body.error}: ${body.message}`);
console.log("Sent:", body.messageId);

That uses the fetch built into Node.js 18 and later, so there's nothing to install. Check your inbox, and your spam folder the first time.

3. Send from your own domain

When you're ready to email your users, verify your domain on the Domains page. Sankofa gives you three DNS records to add. Once they're in, you can send from any address on that domain:

await fetch("https://api.trysankofa.com/v1/emails", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANKOFA_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: "Acme <orders@acme.com.gh>",
    to: "customer@example.com",
    subject: "Your order has shipped",
    html: "<p>Your order is on its way.</p>",
    text: "Your order is on its way.",
  }),
});

Each recipient uses one credit. If a send fails, the credit comes back automatically.

4. Templates, and sending to many people

For emails you send repeatedly, save a template with {{placeholders}}:

await fetch("https://api.trysankofa.com/v1/templates", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANKOFA_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    name: "order-shipped",
    subject: "Your order {{order}} has shipped",
    text: "Hi {{name}}, your order {{order}} is on its way.",
  }),
});

Then send it to up to 500 people in one request. Each person gets their own copy with their own values filled in:

const result = await fetch("https://api.trysankofa.com/v1/emails/bulk", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: {
    Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.SANKOFA_API_KEY}`,
    "Content-Type": "application/json",
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    from: "Acme <orders@acme.com.gh>",
    templateName: "order-shipped",
    recipients: [
      { to: "ama@example.com", templateData: { name: "Ama", order: "A-1042" } },
      { to: "kofi@example.com", templateData: { name: "Kofi", order: "A-1043" } },
    ],
  }),
}).then((r) => r.json());

for (const r of result.results) console.log(r.to, r.status, r.error ?? "");

If one recipient fails (say, an address that bounced before), the rest still go out, and you're not charged for the failure.

5. Know when emails are delivered

Register a webhook on the Webhooks page, and Sankofa will POST delivery events to your server: delivered, bounced, opened, clicked and so on. Each request is signed, so check the signature before trusting it:

import crypto from "node:crypto";

export function isFromSankofa(rawBody, signatureHeader, secret) {
  const parts = Object.fromEntries(signatureHeader.split(",").map((p) => p.split("=")));
  if (!parts.t || !parts.v1) return false;
  if (Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(parts.t)) > 300) return false; // reject old requests

  const expected = crypto.createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${parts.t}.${rawBody}`).digest();
  const given = Buffer.from(parts.v1, "hex");
  return given.length === expected.length && crypto.timingSafeEqual(given, expected);
}

Pass it the raw request body (before JSON parsing) and the X-Webhook-Signature header.

Bonus: let your AI assistant send email

Sankofa has an MCP server, so tools like Claude Code and Cursor can send email and check delivery for you. Create a separate API key for the agent and give it a daily limit, so it can never send more than you allow:

claude mcp add --transport http sankofa https://api.trysankofa.com/mcp \
  --header "Authorization: Bearer esk_your_agent_key"

Then you can ask, "email the team that the deploy is done", and it will.

Wrapping up

That covers most of what an app needs: test sends, your own domain, templates, bulk sends and delivery tracking. The docs cover the rest, including attachments and receiving replies.

It's early days, so I'd really value feedback, especially from anyone building in Ghana or elsewhere in West Africa. What do you use for email today, and what would make you switch?

The first 20 developers get 200 free emails to try it.
